summary: The cellular Multimedia Messaging Service (MMS) is similar to Internet mail but differs in key ways, such as headers beginning with X-Mms-. This document specifies how to exchange messages between MMS and Internet mail. It is standards-track.

plainLanguage.summary: Picture messages on phones and email are cousins that speak slightly different languages. This is the translator between them.

subtitle: How a phone's multimedia messages are translated to and from ordinary Internet email, header by header.

tldr.problem: The cellular Multimedia Messaging Service (MMS) is similar to Internet mail but uses its own X-Mms-* headers and plain-text reports, so the two cannot exchange messages directly.
tldr.mechanism: An MMS Relay/Server acts as a gateway over SMTP. It maps each MMS information element to an SMTP envelope value or an Internet message header, and converts delivery and read reports between the two formats.
tldr.outcome: MMS systems can exchange messages with Internet mail, except that reply charging and sender address hiding are not supported because of their risk.

facts.label: Max Received headers
facts.value: Local limit, should be at least 100

today: RFC 4356 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It still defines the mapping between MMS and Internet mail.

sections.title: Scope and the MM3 Interface
sections.content:
RFC 4356 describes how to exchange messages between Multimedia Messaging Service (MMS) systems and Internet mail systems, meaning SMTP and the Internet message format. It covers translating message formats, message header elements, delivery reports and message disposition reports.

MMS specifications name their interfaces MMx. MM1 is the client-server interface, MM4 is the server-server interface, and MM3 is the interface to external, non-MMS systems. This document uses MM3 from the MMS system's point of view. It also covers voice messages defined by the Voice Profile for Internet Mail (VPIM), so an MMS system can exchange voice messages with a voice mail system.

All MM3 Stage 2 functions are supported except reply charging and sender address hiding. Other uses of MM3, such as SMS interworking, are out of scope. The reader is assumed to know the MMS Stage 1, 2 and 3 documents and the SMTP and message format RFCs.
sections.plainLanguage: Phones send picture messages one way and computers send email another way. This document is the rulebook for a go-between that passes messages from one side to the other.

sections.title: How the Gateway Works
sections.content:
The interworking happens between an MMS Relay/Server and an external server, using native SMTP. Information elements travel as standard Internet message header fields and SMTP elements. SMTP extensions carry features such as delivery reports, message expiration and discovery of optional features.

Going from MMS to Internet mail, the Relay/Server MUST convert the message if required and comply with SMTP. It SHOULD use the message's information elements to build the header fields and SMTP envelope values. Delivery and read report messages SHOULD become standard multipart/report messages.

Going the other way, the Relay/Server converts incoming control information into MMS information elements. Standard report messages MAY become delivery or read reports, and implementations MUST generate standard Internet delivery and disposition reports for received Internet messages as appropriate. Headers not listed in the mapping table SHOULD be passed unaltered.
sections.plainLanguage: The go-between reads each message, rewrites the labels on the outside so the other side understands them, and passes it on. Anything it does not need to change, it leaves alone.

sections.title: Mapping Headers and Envelope Values
sections.content:
Table 1 of the RFC lists each MMS information element beside its SMTP element, its Internet header and its X-Mms- header. When converting from MMS to Internet format, headers that only matter inside MMS, such as X-Mms-3GPP-MMS-Version, X-Mms-Message-Type and X-Mms-Transaction-Id, SHOULD be removed. Message-Id, Subject and (preferably) Content-Type are kept.

Recipients go into the SMTP envelope as RCPT TO values and also appear in To: or Cc:. If no address header is present, a To: header such as undisclosed-recipients:; SHOULD be created. Addresses must be fully qualified domains; an unqualified E.164 number must not be used. The sender goes in From: and, for user-generated messages, in MAIL FROM. For all automatically generated messages, MAIL FROM MUST be null (<>) because of the risk of mail loops.

Other mappings include expiry, which becomes the SMTP DELIVER-BY extension with by-mode R; delivery report requests, which become the DSN extension with the original recipient as ORCPT; read reply requests, which become Disposition-Notification-To:; and priority, which becomes Importance:. Characters outside 7-bit US-ASCII in headers must be encoded, and UTF-16 body text MUST be translated to UTF-8 or another suitable charset.
sections.plainLanguage: Each kind of message has its own set of labels. The go-between swaps each label for the matching one on the other side, and throws away labels the other side would not understand.

sections.title: Internet Mail to MMS and Resent Messages
sections.content:
Coming from the Internet, the gateway keeps Message-Id, To:, Cc:, From: and Subject, and adds MMS headers such as X-Mms-3GPP-MMS-Version. Every recipient in the SMTP envelope is a recipient of the message. Recipients that appear only in headers MUST be ignored, and envelope-only recipients are treated as blind (Bcc) recipients and not added to headers unless there is only one recipient in total. A null return path may produce X-Mms-Message-Class: auto, and a non-null one may produce personal.

Priority is mapped as High, Normal or Low in X-Mms-Priority, from either Importance: or the older non-standard X-Priority: (values 1 and 2 are High, 3 is Normal, 4 and 5 are Low). If both headers are present, Importance: is used. Normal priority omits the header.

Resending history is translated between MMS X-Mms-Previously-Sent-By and X-Mms-Previously-Sent-Date-and-Time headers, which are numbered starting at 0 for the original submission, and Internet Resent- header blocks. The RFC includes a worked example in both directions, and notes that the MMS date format is HTTP-date while Internet mail uses date-time.

Messages containing a Sensitivity: header MUST NOT be sent to an MMS system, since sensitivity is not an MMS feature. The negative delivery status report MUST include the extended status code 5.6.0.
sections.plainLanguage: When a letter has been forwarded several times, each forwarding is written down in order, with number 0 for the very first sender. The go-between copies that list into the format the other side likes.

sections.title: Delivery and Read Reports
sections.content:
Internet mail reports use the multipart/report type, a two- or three-part message with a structured, easy-to-parse part. MMS reports are plain text with no defined structure, which makes converting an MMS report into a standard one hard. A conforming implementation MUST convert reports in both directions and MUST generate reports for messages received from either side.

A report built from an MMS report has a text/plain first part for people, a report/delivery-status or report/disposition-notification second part, and an optional third part of type message/rfc822 with the original headers. The DSN-Gateway: field in delivery reports MUST be created.

For delivery status, the MMS X-Mms-Status values map to DSN Action values: retrieved and rejected to delivered, expired and unreachable to failed, deferred to delayed (a MAY), and indeterminate to relayed. In the other direction, deferred MUST NOT be used, so DSNs with Action delayed are ignored. For read reports, X-Mms-Read-Status of read maps to the disposition type displayed, and deleting without reading maps to deleted.

On delivery: in Internet mail, delivery means acceptance by the final server, but an MMS Relay/Server MAY consider a message delivered once it has been sent to the MMS user agent.
sections.plainLanguage: When you send a letter, you can ask for a receipt. Phones write receipts in plain sentences and email writes them in a strict form, so the go-between rewrites each receipt for the other side.

sections.title: Security and Registration
sections.content:
The RFC limits its security discussion to what is specific to this mapping. When a message uses end-to-end security such as OpenPGP or S/MIME, servers MUST be careful not to destroy the integrity of the protected content, for example by altering text inside a signed region while mapping.

Some MMS features carry inherently more risk, including reply charging and sender address hiding, and support for them is not included. Reply charging SHOULD NOT be honored on this interface until security issues are addressed, because misapplied reply charging may cause incorrect billing, and messages with a reply-charging usage request SHOULD be rejected. A message with X-Mms-Sender-Visibility of Hide SHOULD be rejected.

For IANA, "MMS" was added as a "WITH protocol type" in the MAIL Parameters registry, with the description "Multimedia Messaging Service". A gateway puts it in the with clause of the Received: header it adds.
sections.plainLanguage: If a letter is sealed or signed, the go-between must not scribble on it. It also refuses features that could cause wrong bills or hide who sent a message.

items.label: DELIVER-BY
items.desc: Remaining time goes in the SMTP DELIVER-BY extension with by-mode R.

items.label: DSN
items.desc: Becomes the SMTP DSN extension, with the recipient as ORCPT.

items.label: Disposition-Notification-To
items.desc: Read reply request becomes an MDN request header.

items.label: Importance
items.desc: High and Low are mapped; Normal omits the header.

items.label: MAIL FROM
items.desc: Class auto requires a null MAIL FROM.
